name: The Anne Frank Chestnut Sapling

location.address: Idaho Anne Frank Human Rights Memorial, 770 S 8th St, Boise, Idaho 83702 (also cited as 800 S 8th St by the City of Boise's own page; the memorial address is disputed between two of its own official pages, not between our sources and a third party)
location.neighbourhood: Near Boise State University / Boise River Greenbelt, downtown Boise

verified_sources: https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2009/oct/28/a-living-connection/ (Spokesman-Review, 28 Oct 2009: Boise named one of 11 US sites to receive a grafted sapling from the Amsterdam Anne Frank tree, sapling then about 3ft tall, to undergo a 2-year quarantine at a city tree nursery before planting on a grassy berm near the Frank Church memorial tablet, in sightline of the Anne Frank statue)

https://www.wassmuthcenter.org/about-the-anne-frank-memorial/ (Wassmuth Center for Human Rights, co-operator of the memorial: confirms the sapling as a prominent installation; confirms the memorial is free, open year-round dawn to dusk, at 770 S 8th St)

https://www.cityofboise.org/departments/parks-and-recreation/parks/idaho-anne-frank-human-rights-memorial/ (City of Boise's own parks page: confirms the sapling 'is planted in the Memorial', address given as 800 S 8th St)

https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:AnneFrankHumanRightsMemorialSapling.jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0 photograph dated 13 May 2017, captioned 'a sapling from the Anne Frank tree, one of only 11 in the U.S., at the Anne Frank Human Rights Memorial in Boise, Idaho' -- direct dated evidence the tree was alive and already an established juvenile by 2017)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Frank_Human_Rights_Memorial (corroborates: sapling is one of only 11 Anne Frank saplings in the US, a prominent installation at the memorial)
access: Free, public memorial and park. Open year-round, seven days a week, dawn to dusk (Wassmuth Center for Human Rights, which co-maintains the site with the City of Boise). No admission fee; guided tours available with 48 hours' notice.
transport: Downtown Boise, near Boise State University and the Boise River Greenbelt; walkable from downtown.
story:
Anne Frank could see one tree from the annex, and this is its child. Chestnuts from that Amsterdam horse chestnut were raised into saplings, eleven of which were planted in the United States, one of them here. The parent, roughly 150 to 170 years old, came down in a storm in August 2010, so this graft has now outlived the tree it came from.

Nothing about its size or age argues for the trip. It reached Boise around October 2009 at about three feet tall and had to sit out roughly two years of quarantine in a city nursery before it could go in the ground. Nobody has published a firm planting date, so we date it loosely, somewhere between eleven and fifteen years old. If you know the year it went in, tell us.

The lineage is the whole case, and the company it keeps says what the distributors thought they were doing: the other American recipients include the White House, the 9/11 Memorial in New York and Central High School in Little Rock.

It grows on a grassy berm behind a low iron fence, ringed with pink roses, across from the plaza where a bronze Anne Frank stands at a window looking out. The memorial is free and open dawn to dusk, every day of the year.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the low iron fence and the ring of pink roses around it, and by its size: a young chestnut, not a big one. It stands on the grassy berm across from the plaza with the bronze statue of Anne Frank at her window.

name: The Idaho Champion Kentucky Coffeetree of Julia Davis Park

location.address: Julia Davis Park, Boise, Idaho (exact spot within the park not independently pinned this pass; same public park as the already-published boi_001 Bur Oak)

verified_sources: https://www.newsbf.com/news/201511/20151124idahobigtreelist.pdf (Idaho Big Tree Program, University of Idaho Extension, official state champion-tree register, January 2014 edition, page 19: Gymnocladus dioicus, Kentucky coffeetree, STATE record, 41in DBH, 129in circumference, 74ft tall, 12ft 1/4-avg-crown, 215 points, 'Julia Davis Park, Boise, Ada Co., ID', nominated by R. Mahoney, 1986)

https://sites.stat.washington.edu/jaw/CAW/june-2019-id-registry-big-trees.pdf (Idaho's Registry of Champion Big Trees, 13 June 2019 edition, University of Idaho Extension, page 9: identical figures -- 41in DBH, 129in circumference, 74ft, 12ft crown, 215 points, Julia Davis Park, Boise, Ada Co., ID, R. Mahoney, 1986 -- the same record still current five years after the first document checked here, i.e. not delisted as dead or removed in the intervening period)

https://www.uidaho.edu/extension/forestry/big-trees (Idaho Big Tree Program's own general programme page, same institution/register; cited the same way boi_001 and boi_002 already cite it in this city's published file)
access: Free, public city park (same park as boi_001, the Julia Davis Park Bur Oak). Also home to the Boise Art Museum, Zoo Boise and Idaho State Historical Museum.
story:
The largest Kentucky coffeetree in Idaho grows in a city park that also holds an art museum and a zoo. It stands 74 feet tall with a trunk 328 centimetres round, and it has held the state record since a University of Idaho forester nominated it in 1986.

It is an odd thing to be champion of. The species belongs to the Midwest rather than to the high desert, and its name is literal: settlers roasted the seeds as a substitute for coffee. Raw, the seeds and pods are mildly toxic, which is why the seedless cultivars are the ones cities plant today. The register does not record which kind this one is.

Everything we know about it comes from one place. The Idaho Big Tree Program printed identical figures in its 2014 and 2019 editions, five years apart: 41 inches through the trunk at chest height, 74 feet tall, 215 points. That is one register republished rather than two sources agreeing, so the entry is flagged. What the repetition does tell us is that nobody struck the tree off in between.

Nobody has dated it. The register gives no age for any of its cultivated trees, so the field stays empty rather than filled with a guess. If you know when it went in, tell us. It shares Julia Davis Park with the champion bur oak, which makes the two an easy pair in one walk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 74 feet, and by the trunk, 328 centimetres round: no other Kentucky coffeetree in Idaho is bigger. It stands in Julia Davis Park, the same park as the champion bur oak.
